look_here_first: Start with several mature, NOT juvenile, bristle-tipped leaves. Then check terminal buds (small, scales distinctly ciliate toward tips) and the mature acorn: a relatively deep goblet/cup-shaped cup commonly enclosing 1/3–1/2 of the nut. Compare against Shumard oak's generally larger, shallower-cupped fruits.

key_traits.label: Bark
key_traits.text: Gray and smooth to black and furrowed.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Broadly elliptic to obovate/circular; usually 7–9 lobes; lobe tips acute to acuminate with numerous awns/bristles; surfaces mostly glabrous and often glossy.

key_traits.label: Acorn
key_traits.text: Biennial; cup usually goblet- to cup-shaped and covers roughly one-third to one-half of the nut.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: FNA adult leaf blade usually 55–100 mm long; glabrous to small tufts beneath at vein axils

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: terminal buds gray-brown/reddish-brown, scales ciliate toward apex

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: mature cup commonly 5–11.5 mm deep and 10–18 mm wide; shape/depth best read on attached ripe acorns

key_traits.label: Joey field note
key_traits.text: Joey's landscaping video gives a direct crown-and-lobed-leaf field view of Texas red oak. A second Edwards Plateau frame shows a rock-wall/chasmophyte oak that Joey calls 'probably Quercus buckleyi'; retain that second frame only as tentative habitat context, not as a definitive species diagnostic.
